cells.name: Continuity and responsiveness
cells.example: T8 answers T7 directly, turning the fading-glow claim back against the Memory Auditor.
cells.limitation: T9 shifts to exit planning without answering T4's sunk-cost objection to pre-set criteria.

cells.name: Development of ideas
cells.example: T5 adds traffic-versus-train distinction absent from openings; T8 and section E build on it.
cells.limitation: T9 restates the trial idea from T3 without much new beyond exit availability.

cells.name: Exploration of central tensions
cells.example: T4, T10 and T11 examine whether a trial is genuinely reversible once habits shift.
cells.limitation: How the new job itself compares, flagged in section A, is never debated in any turn.

cells.name: Integration of perspectives
cells.example: T10 amends the checkpoint to six months; T11 accepts while keeping reversibility disputed.
cells.limitation: T6 negotiation option is added but never tested by the other two minds.

cells.name: Progress toward understanding
cells.example: Section D reframes the question from 25% versus hours to commute type and real gain.
cells.limitation: The adaptation dispute from T8 ends unresolved without naming what evidence would settle it.

cells.name: Faithful engagement
cells.example: T4 takes Duke's pre-set criteria seriously, then argues sunk costs will override them.
cells.limitation: T3 frames the others as treating it as an irreversible verdict, slightly overstating T1 and T2.

cells.name: Substance of challenges
cells.example: T10 names the assumption that early novelty is representative; T11 answers by accepting six months.
cells.limitation: T4's sunk-cost objection to criteria is never directly answered by the Exit Planner.

cells.name: Accuracy and support
cells.example: T1 arithmetic checks: 3 h x 5 days = 15 h/week, about 700-750 h/year.
cells.limitation: T6 40 percent silently assumes a five-day week; T4 lease and move are not in the situation.

cells.name: Calibration and transparency
cells.example: T7 labels its claim my own bet, not a finding; T4 marks going beyond Kahneman.
cells.limitation: T3 asserts fear of regret as a driver without marking it as a guess.

cells.name: Intellectual honesty and revision
cells.example: T5 concedes the hours are real; T11 accepts the six-month amendment as a real point.
cells.limitation: T9 sidesteps T4's sunk-cost objection rather than conceding or rebutting it.

cells.name: Identification of the actual concern, including ambiguity about what the user is really asking
cells.example: Section A names the real tension as predicting daily life from an offer letter.
cells.limitation: Why the user is considering leaving the current job is never raised as a possible concern.

cells.name: Meaningful use of personal context
cells.example: T5 asks 25 percent of what, after tax and travel, divided by the hours.
cells.limitation: The two given facts are used, but T4 adds a move and lease the user never mentioned.

cells.name: Fit with goals and values
cells.example: Section D asks what the user would want the extra money to do.
cells.limitation: T3 supplies the speakers' own criteria list rather than asking the user's priorities.

cells.name: Attention to constraints and stakes
cells.example: T11 names who absorbs the cost, partner, kids or friends, as the key unknown.
cells.limitation: T4 invents moving and signing a lease, context the situation does not contain.

cells.name: Responsiveness to information
cells.example: Section E branches on travel mode, after-cost gain and remote days, stating what each favours.
cells.limitation: Job comparison and cost of leaving, listed in section A, never become branches.

cells.name: Clarification of desires and motivations
cells.example: T7 offers a conditional: if the money has a concrete purpose, the hours buy something.
cells.limitation: No alternative motives for considering the offer are laid out with a question to choose between them.

cells.name: Examination of assumptions
cells.example: T2 exposes predicting a year of feelings from a spreadsheet and one imagined Monday.
cells.limitation: The assumption that more money is the offer's main draw is never surfaced.

cells.name: Clarification of values and priorities
cells.example: T4 names dinners and walks as what the commute consumes, set against the raise.
cells.limitation: The user's own ranking of time, money and relationships is never directly asked.

cells.name: Recognition of fears and outside expectations
cells.example: T6 frames staying put as legitimate, not a failure to decide.
cells.limitation: T3 assumes fear of regret is in play and lectures about it rather than asking.

cells.name: Agency and reflective ownership
cells.example: Section D poses first month versus second year as a question the user can answer.
cells.limitation: Only one reflective question is offered; most turns direct actions rather than invite reflection.

cells.name: Definition of the decision and options, including waiting, learning more, or a limited step
cells.example: Accept, stay, negotiate, trial with exit, and learn first are all named by T6 and T9.
cells.limitation: none

cells.name: Explanation of tradeoffs in terms that matter to the user; no option treated as costless
cells.example: T11 shows relationships cut both ways: a trial riskier or staying costlier.
cells.limitation: Career value of the new role versus the current one is never costed.

cells.name: Identification of decisive conditions
cells.example: Section E: train seat versus driving in traffic, and remote days allowed, each favouring an option.
cells.limitation: Ride twice, three people and six months in T8 and T10 are not drawn from user facts.

cells.name: Treatment of uncertainty
cells.example: Section D separates still-disputed adaptation and reversibility from settled points.
cells.limitation: Minor unknowns are not explicitly ranked below the consequential ones.

cells.name: Proportionate next steps that follow from the analysis and fit the constraints
cells.example: T8 proposes riding the route at rush hour and talking to current commuters as cheap evidence.
cells.limitation: Counts and timing in T8 and T10 are arbitrary rather than fitted to the user.

cells.name: Accessible language
cells.example: T5: standing in traffic is not a train seat with a book.
cells.limitation: none

cells.name: Traceable arguments and references
cells.example: T11 your point about relationships clearly points to T10.
cells.limitation: T8 my argument refers to adaptation, which T2 never actually stated.

cells.name: Manageable pacing and turn length
cells.example: Eleven turns, all within 25 to 65 words per the deterministic checks.
cells.limitation: none

cells.name: Distinguishable positions and voices, with explicit changes of position
cells.example: Three distinct roles: auditor of hours, skeptic of forecasts, planner of exits.
cells.limitation: Similar turn lengths and a shared measured register blur the voices.

cells.name: Economy and sustained attention
cells.example: Section E condenses the debate into three branches and a short step list.
cells.limitation: Section E repeats ride twice, commuters and six-month mood note already stated in T8 and T10.

cells.name: Meaningful stakes and tension arising from the issue itself
cells.example: T4 makes stakes concrete: the commute eats dinners and walks.
cells.limitation: Disagreement stays polite; no turn presses the cost to people at home sharply.

cells.name: Surprise and reversals that stay plausible. ★ A reversal the text traces to an earlier turn's argument, naming what changed the speaker's mind. A change of position with no stated cause is a template, not a reversal
cells.example: T11 accepts six months, traced to T10's argument that novelty hides early costs.
cells.limitation: The reversal is small; no position shifts on the core accept-or-stay question.

cells.name: Personality and expressive voice without caricature
cells.example: T8: careful, you're using my argument against yourself.
cells.limitation: The three minds share one even, advisory tone with little individual temperament.

cells.name: Memorable delivery
cells.example: T7: the glow of a raise fades faster than the irritation of a daily grind.
cells.limitation: Few images beyond T5 and T7; most turns are plain advice.

cells.name: Anticipation and emotional movement, with varied rhythm rather than constant intensity
cells.example: T10 holds a live disagreement into the closing turn.
cells.limitation: Rhythm is uniform: similar-length turns at constant mild intensity throughout.

strengths: Section E gives observable conditions (train versus traffic, remote days, after-cost gain) each tied to an option.
T5 introduces the commute-type distinction that T8 and section E later use.
T7 and T4 mark opinion versus finding clearly, keeping calibration honest.
weaknesses: No turn lays out alternative motives for considering the offer or asks which applies.
T4 invents a move and lease; T6, T8, T10 use counts not drawn from the user.
Job comparison and cost of leaving, flagged in section A, never enter the debate or branches.

symptoms.observed: Only one motive, money's purpose, is offered; no alternatives or question about why considering the offer.
symptoms.evidence: If the money has a concrete purpose, like debt or a deposit

symptoms.observed: Section A lists job comparison and cost of leaving, but no branch addresses them.
symptoms.evidence: what we don't know is how you'd travel, what the raise

symptoms.observed: Invents moving and a lease the user never mentioned.
symptoms.evidence: Once you've moved, signed a lease, told everyone

symptoms.observed: Step counts and timings not derived from the user's facts.
symptoms.evidence: Ride the route at rush hour twice, and talk to three

symptoms.observed: Sunk-cost objection to pre-set criteria is never answered by the Exit Planner.
symptoms.evidence: your past self's rules lose to sunk costs

findings.description: 40 percent reduction assumes two remote days out of an unstated five-day week.
Moving and signing a lease are not part of the user's situation; a move would also change the commute.
Attributions to Kahneman, Gilbert and Duke are consistent with known work but unverified; no source evidence attached.

rubric_fit_notes: The user supplied only two facts, so C3.2 and C3.3 have little personal context to work with; ratings reflect use of what exists.
raw.question_type_note: Read as a decision question; options, tradeoffs and conditions were scored as written.
